query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The improved corrosion resistance of steels in chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments is due to a microstructure‐mediated mechanism in which an ultrafine-grained structure—with a high density of high-angle grain boundaries—accelerates chromium diffusion to the surface, thereby rapidly forming and repairing a protective Cr‐enriched passive film.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional stainless or duplex steel used in such applications with a typical coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply high-pressure torsion (or another severe plastic deformation process) to the steel to refine the grain size while keeping the chemical composition unchanged.
generation.conditions: Corrosion testing performed in environments simulating chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, for example in controlled high-temperature, high-pressure aqueous media (e.g., chloride-containing or simulated primary water conditions) where the passivation behavior of the steel is critical.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain refinement that increases the fraction of high-angle grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: High-angle grain boundaries act as fast diffusion paths for Cr atoms. This enhanced diffusion accelerates the formation and continual repair of a chromium-enriched passive film, which protects the underlying steel from aggressive corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical corrosive conditions, the ultrafine-grained (processed) steel will exhibit a more noble (less negative) corrosion potential and a lower corrosion current density compared to the baseline coarse-grained steel, indicating improved corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: Steel in its as-received (conventionally processed, coarse-grained) condition.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic benefit is expected to be operative under conditions typical for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, where temperature, pressure, and corrosive media reflect those environments; deviations in alloy composition or extreme environmental variations may limit the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance is not predetermined and may depend on the specific steel composition, the degree of grain refinement achieved, and the test environment details.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples: one set processed by high-pressure torsion to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure, and a control set in the conventional coarse-grained state. Expose both sets to identical, simulated chemical-processing/nuclear-power environments (e.g., high-temperature, high-pressure aqueous solutions with controlled chloride content).
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization tests to measure corrosion potential and corrosion current density
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or other surface analytical techniques to verify the Cr concentration in the passive film
Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM and grain size analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained samples do not show a statistically significant shift toward a more noble corrosion potential, a lower corrosion current density, and enhanced Cr enrichment in the passive film compared to the coarse-grained control, then the hypothesis that grain refinement accelerates Cr diffusion and passive film formation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed.
